In [[mathematics]], a '''Grassmannian''' <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math>, also known as a '''Grassmann manifold''', is a [[differentiable manifold]] that parameterizes the set of all <math>k</math>-[[dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[linear subspace]]s of an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[vector space]] <math>V</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math> that has a [[Differential structure|differentiable structure]]. For example, the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}_1(V)</math> is the space of lines through the origin in <math>V</math>, so it is the same as the [[projective space]] <math>\mathbf{P}(V)</math> of one dimension lower than <math>V</math>.{{sfn|Lee|2012|p=22|loc=Example 1.36}}{{sfn|Shafarevich|2013|p=42|loc=Example 1.24}}
When <math>V</math> is a [[real number|real]] or [[complex number|complex]] vector space, Grassmannians are [[compact space|compact]] [[smooth manifold]]s, of dimension <math>k(n-k)</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Milnor|Stasheff|1974}}, pp. 57–59.</ref> In general they have the structure of a nonsingular [[projective algebraic variety]]. The Grassmannian is named for the German polymath, linguist and mathematician [[Hermann Grassmann]], who introduced the concept to mathematics.

== History ==
The earliest work on a non-trivial Grassmannian was by [[Julius Plücker]], who studied the set of projective lines in real projective 3-space, which is equivalent to <math>\mathbf{Gr}_2(\mathbf{R}^4)</math>, parameterizing them by what are now called [[Plücker coordinates]]. [[Hermann Grassmann]] later generalized the concept.

Notations for Grassmannians vary between authors; they include <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math>, <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,V)</math>,<math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(n)</math>, <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,n)</math> to denote the Grassmannian of <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of an <math>n</math>-dimensional vector space <math>V</math>.

==Motivation==
By giving a collection of subspaces of a vector space a [[topological]] structure, it is possible to talk about a [[continuous (topology)|continuous]] choice of subspaces or [[open set|open]] and [[closed set|closed]] collections of subspaces. Giving them the further structure of a [[differentiable manifold]] enables smooth choices of subspace.

A natural example comes from [[tangent bundle]]s of smooth manifolds embedded in a [[Euclidean space]]. Given a manifold <math>M</math> of dimension <math>k</math> embedded in <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math>. At each point <math> x\in M</math>, the [[tangent space]] to <math>M</math> can be considered as a subspace of the tangent space of <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math>, which is also just <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math>. The [[function (mathematics)|map]] assigning to <math> x</math> its tangent space defines a map from {{mvar|M}} to <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>. (In order to do this, the tangent space at each <math>x \in M</math> must be translated so that it passes through the origin rather than <math>x</math>, and hence defines a <math>k</math>-dimensional vector subspace. This idea is similar to the [[Gauss map]] for surfaces in a 3-dimensional space.)

This can be extended to all [[vector bundle]]s over a manifold <math>M</math>, so that every vector bundle generates a continuous map from <math>M</math> to a suitably generalised Grassmannian—although various embedding [[theorem]]s must be [[mathematical proof|proved]] to show this. The properties of vector bundles are thus related to the properties of the corresponding maps. In particular vector bundles inducing [[homotopic]] maps to the Grassmannian are [[isomorphic]]. Here the definition of [[homotopy]] relies on a notion of continuity, and hence a [[Topology optimization|topology]].

==Low dimensions==
For {{math|1=''k'' = 1}}, the Grassmannian {{math|'''Gr'''(1, ''n'')}} is the space of lines through the origin in {{mvar|n}}-space, so it is the same as the [[projective space]] <math>\mathbf{P}^{n-1}</math> of {{math|''n'' − 1}} dimensions.

For {{math|1=''k'' = 2}}, the Grassmannian is the space of all 2-dimensional planes containing the origin. In [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean]] 3-space, a plane containing the origin is completely characterized by the single line through the origin that is [[perpendicular]] to that plane (and vice versa); hence the spaces {{math|'''Gr'''(2, 3)}}, {{math|'''Gr'''(1, 3)}}, and {{math|'''P'''<sup>2</sup>}} (the [[projective plane]]) may all be identified with each other.

The simplest Grassmannian that is not a [[projective space]] is {{math|'''Gr'''(2, 4)}}.

== Differentiable manifold ==

To endow <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> with the structure of a differentiable manifold, a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for <math>V</math> must be chosen. This is equivalent to identifying <math>V</math> with <math>K^n</math>, with the standard basis denoted <math>(e_1, \dots, e_n)</math>, viewed as column vectors. Then for any <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace <math>w\subset V</math>, viewed as an element of <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math>, a basis can be found consisting of <math>k</math> [[linearly independent]] column vectors <math>(W_1, \dots, W_k)</math>. The [[homogeneous coordinates]] of the element <math> w \in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> consist of the elements of the <math>n\times k</math> maximal [[rank of a matrix|rank]] rectangular [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] <math>W</math> whose <math>i</math>-th column vector is <math>W_i</math>, <math>i = 1, \dots, k </math>. Since the choice of basis is arbitrary, two such maximal rank rectangular matrices <math>W</math> and <math>\tilde{W}</math> represent the same element <math>w \in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> [[if and only if]] 
::<math>\tilde{W} = W g</math> 
for some element <math>g \in GL(k, K)</math> of the [[general linear group]] of [[invertible matrix|invertible]] <math>k\times k </math> matrices with entries in <math>K</math>. This defines an [[equivalence relation]] between <math>n\times k</math> matrices <math>W</math> of rank <math>k</math>, for which the equivalence classes are denoted <math>[W]</math>.

A coordinate atlas ensures that for any <math>n \times k</math> homogeneous coordinate matrix <math>W</math>, [[elementary matrix|elementary column operations]] can be applied (essentially multiplying <math>W</math> by a sequence of elements <math>g \in GL(k, K)</math>) to obtain its [[echelon form|reduced column echelon form]]. If the first <math>k</math> rows of <math>W</math> are linearly independent, the result has the form
::<math>\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ & 1 \\ & & \ddots \\ & & & 1 \\ a_{1,1} & \cdots & \cdots & a_{1,k} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ a_{n-k,1} & \cdots & \cdots & a_{n-k,k} \end{bmatrix}</math>
and the <math>(n-k)\times k</math> affine coordinate matrix
<math>A</math> with entries <math>(a_{ij})</math> determines <math>w</math>. In general, the first <math>k</math> rows need not be independent, but since <math>W</math> has maximal rank <math>k</math>, an ordered set of integers <math>1 \le i_1 < \cdots < i_k \le n</math> exists such that the <math>k \times k</math> submatrix <math>W_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> whose rows are the <math>(i_1, \ldots, i_k)</math>-th rows of <math>W</math> is [[singular matrix|nonsingular]]. Column operations can reduce this submatrix to the [[identity matrix]], and the remaining entries uniquely determine <math>w</math>. This gives the following definition:

For each ordered set of integers <math>1 \le i_1 < \cdots < i_k \le n</math>, let <math>U_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> a set of elements <math>w\in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> exists for which, for any choice of homogeneous coordinate matrix <math>W</math>, the <math>k\times k</math> submatrix <math>W_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> whose <math>j</math>-th row is the <math>i_j</math>-th row of <math>W</math> is nonsingular. The affine coordinate functions on <math>U_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> are then defined as the entries of the <math>(n-k)\times k </math> matrix <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> whose rows are those of the matrix <math>W W^{-1}_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> complementary to <math> (i_1, \dots, i_k)</math>, written in the same order. The choice of homogeneous <math>n \times k</math> coordinate matrix <math>W</math> in <math>[W]</math> representing the element <math>w\in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> does not affect the values of the affine coordinate matrix <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> representing {{mvar|w}} on the coordinate neighbourhood <math>U_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math>. Moreover, the coordinate matrices <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> may take arbitrary values, and they define a [[diffeomorphism]] from <math>U_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> to the space of <math>K</math>-valued <math>(n-k)\times k </math> matrices. This can be denoted by

::<math>\hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k} := W (W_{i_1, \dots , i_k})^{-1}</math>

the homogeneous coordinate matrix having the identity matrix as the <math>k \times k</math> submatrix with rows <math>(i_1, \dots, i_k)</math> and the affine coordinate matrix <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> in the consecutive complementary rows. On the overlap <math> U_{i_1, \dots, i_k} \cap U_{j_1, \dots, j_k}</math> between any two such coordinate neighborhoods, the affine coordinate matrix values <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> and <math>A^{j_1, \dots, j_k}</math> are related by the transition relations 
::<math > \hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k} W_{i_1, \dots, i_k} = \hat{A}^{j_1, \dots, j_k} W_{j_1, \dots, j_k},</math>

where both <math>W_{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math> and <math>W_{j_1, \dots, j_k}</math> are invertible. This may equivalently be written as
::<math > \hat{A}^{j_1, \dots, j_k} = \hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k} (\hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k}_{j_1, \dots, j_k})^{-1},</math>
where <math> \hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k}_{j_1, \dots, j_k} </math> is the invertible <math>k \times k </math> matrix whose <math>l</math>th row is the <math>j_l</math>th row of <math>\hat{A}^{i_1, \dots, i_k}</math>. The transition functions are therefore rational in the matrix elements of <math>A^{i_1, \dots, i_k} </math>, and <math>\{U_{i_1, \dots, i_k}, A^{i_1, \dots, i_k}\}</math> gives an atlas for <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> as a differentiable manifold and also as an algebraic variety.

== Orthogonal projections ==
An alternative way to define a real or complex Grassmannian as a manifold is to view it as a set of orthogonal [[Projection (linear algebra)|projection operators]].{{sfn|Milnor|Stasheff|1974|p=}}{{page needed|date=January 2026}} For this, a positive definite real or Hermitian [[inner product]] <math>\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle</math> on <math>V</math> can be chosen, depending on whether <math>V</math> is real or complex. A <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace <math>w</math> determines a unique orthogonal projection operator <math>P_w:V\rightarrow V</math> whose [[image (mathematics)|image]] is <math>w\subset V</math> by splitting <math>V</math> into the orthogonal direct sum
::<math>V = w \oplus w^\perp </math>
of <math>w</math> and its orthogonal complement <math>w^\perp</math> and defining
::<math> P_w(v) =\begin{cases} v \quad \text{ if } v \in w \\
    0 \quad \text{ if } v\in w^\perp .
\end{cases} </math> 
Conversely, every projection operator <math>P</math> of rank <math>k</math> defines a subspace <math>w_P := \mathrm{Im}(P)</math> as its image. Since the rank of an orthogonal projection operator equals its [[trace of a matrix|trace]], we can identify the Grassmann manifold <math> \mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> with the set of rank <math>k</math> orthogonal projection operators <math>P</math>:  
::<math> \mathbf{Gr}(k, V) \sim \left\{ P \in \mathrm{End}(V) \mid P = P^2 = P^\dagger,\, \mathrm{tr}(P) = k \right\}.</math>

In particular, taking <math>V = \mathbf{R}^n</math> or <math>V = \mathbf{C}^n</math> gives completely explicit equations for embedding the Grassmannians <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{R}^N) </math>, <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^N) </math> in the space of real or complex <math>n\times n </math> matrices <math>\mathbf{R}^{n \times n}</math>, <math>\mathbf{C}^{n \times n}</math>, respectively.

Since this defines the Grassmannian as a closed subset of the sphere <math>\{X \in \mathrm{End}(V) \mid \mathrm{tr}(XX^\dagger) = k\}</math> the Grassmannian is a [[compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] space. This construction also turns the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> into a [[metric space]] with metric
::<math>d(w, w') := \lVert P_w - P_{w'} \rVert,</math>
for any pair <math> w, w' \subset V</math> of <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces, where {{math|{{norm|⋅}}}} denotes the [[operator norm]]. The exact inner product used does not matter, because a different inner product gives an equivalent norm on <math>V</math>, and hence an equivalent metric.

For the case of real or complex Grassmannians, the following is an equivalent way to express the above construction in terms of matrices.

== Affine algebraic varieties ==
Let <math>M(n, \mathbf{R})</math> denote the space of real <math>n \times n </math> matrices and the subset <math> P(k, n, \mathbf{R})\subset M(n, \mathbf{R})</math> of matrices <math> P \in M(n, \mathbf{R}) </math> that satisfy the three conditions:

* <math>P</math> is a [[projection operator]]: <math>P^2=P</math>.
* <math>P</math> is [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]]: <math>P^T=P</math>.
* <math>P</math> has trace <math>\operatorname{tr}(P)=k</math>.

A bijective correspondence exists between <math> P(k, n, \mathbf{R})</math> and the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{R}^n)</math> of <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math> given by sending <math>P\in P(k, n, \mathbf{R}) </math> to the <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace of <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math> spanned by its columns and, conversely, sending any element <math>w\in\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{R}^n)</math> to the projection matrix
::<math>P_w:= \sum_{i=1}^k w_i w_i^T,</math>

where <math>(w_1, \cdots, w_k)</math> is any orthonormal basis for <math>w\subset\mathbf{R}^n</math>, viewed as real <math>n</math> component column vectors.

An analogous construction applies to the complex Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^n)</math>, identifying it bijectively with the subset <math>P(k, n, \mathbf{C})\subset M(n,\mathbf{C})</math> of complex <math>n \times n </math> matrices <math> P\in M(n,\mathbf{C}) </math> satisfying
* <math>P</math> is a [[projection operator]]: <math>P^2=P</math>.
* <math>P</math> is [[Hermitian matrix|self-adjoint]] (Hermitian): <math>P^\dagger=P</math>.
* <math>P</math> has trace <math>\operatorname{tr}(P)=k</math>,
where the [[Hermitian matrices|self-adjointness]] is with respect to the Hermitian inner product <math> \langle \, \cdot, \cdot \, \rangle </math> in which the standard basis vectors <math>(e_1, \cdots, e_n) </math> are orthonomal. The formula for the orthogonal projection matrix <math>P_w</math> onto the complex <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace <math>w\subset \mathbf{C}^n</math> spanned by the orthonormal (unitary) basis vectors <math>(w_1, \cdots, w_k)</math> is
::<math>P_w:= \sum_{i=1}^k w_i w_i^\dagger.</math>

== Homogeneous space ==
The quickest way of giving the Grassmannian a geometric structure is to express it as a [[homogeneous space]]. The general linear group <math>\mathrm{GL}(V)</math> [[group action|acts]] [[transitive action|transitively]] on the <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>V</math>. Therefore, by choosing a subspace <math>w_0 \subset V</math> of dimension <math>k</math>, any element <math>w\in\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> can be expressed as
:<math> w = g (w_0) </math>
for some group element <math>g \in \mathrm{GL}(V) </math>, where <math>g</math> is determined only up to right multiplication by elements <math>\{h \in H\}</math> of the [[Group action#Orbits and stabilizers|stabilizer]] of <math>w_0</math>:
:<math> H:=\mathrm{stab}(w_0):=\{h\in \mathrm{GL}(V) \,|\, h(w_0)=w_0 \} \subset \mathrm{GL}(V) </math>
under the <math>\mathrm{GL}(V)</math>-action.

<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> can be identified with the quotient space
:<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V) = \mathrm{GL}(V)/H</math>
of [[Coset#Definition|left cosets]] of <math>H</math>.

If the underlying field <math>\mathbf{R}</math> or <math>\mathbf{C}</math> and <math>\mathrm{GL}(V)</math> is considered as a [[Lie group]], this construction makes the Grassmannian a [[smooth manifold]] under the quotient structure. More generally, over a [[ground field]] <math>K</math>, the group <math>\mathrm{GL}(V)</math> is an [[algebraic group]], and this construction shows that the Grassmannian is a [[singular point of an algebraic variety|non-singular]] [[algebraic variety]]. It follows from the existence of the [[Plücker embedding]] that the Grassmannian is [[complete algebraic variety|complete]] as an algebraic variety. In particular, <math>H</math> is a [[Borel subgroup|parabolic subgroup]] of <math>\mathrm{GL}(V)</math>.

Over <math>\mathbf{R}</math> or <math>\mathbf{C}</math> it becomes possible to use smaller groups in this construction. To do this over <math>\mathbf{R}</math>, a Euclidean inner product can be fixed <math>q</math> on <math>V</math>. The real [[orthogonal group]] <math>O(V, q)</math> acts transitively on the set of <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> and the stabiliser of a <math>k</math>-space <math>w_0\subset V</math> is 
:<math>O(w_0, q|_{w_0})\times O(w^\perp_0, q|_{w^\perp_0})</math>,
where <math>w_0^\perp</math> is the orthogonal complement of <math>w_0</math> in <math>V</math>.  This gives an identification as the homogeneous space
:<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V) = O(V, q)/\left(O(w, q|_w)\times O(w^\perp, q|_{w^\perp})\right)</math>.
taking <math>V = \mathbf{R}^n</math> and <math>w_0 = \mathbf{R}^k \subset \mathbf{R}^n</math> (the first <math>k</math> components) gives the isomorphism
:<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k,\mathbf{R}^n) = O(n)/\left(O(k) \times O(n - k)\right).</math>

Over {{math|'''C'''}}, choosing an Hermitian inner product <math>h</math> let the [[unitary group]] <math>U(V, h)</math> act transitively, and analogously
:<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V) = U(V , h)/\left(U(w_0, h|_{w_0}) \times U(w_0^\perp|, h_{w_0^\perp})\right),</math>
or, for <math>V = \mathbf{C}^n</math> and <math>w_0 = \mathbf{C}^k \subset \mathbf{C}^n</math>,
:<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathbf{C}^n) = U(n)/\left(U(k) \times U(n-k)\right).</math>

In particular, this shows that the Grassmannian is [[compact space|compact]], and of (real or complex) dimension {{math|''k''(''n'' − ''k'')}}.

== Scheme ==
In the realm of [[algebraic geometry]], the Grassmannian can be constructed as a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] by expressing it as a [[representable functor]].<ref>{{Cite book | last1=Grothendieck | first1=Alexander | author1-link=Alexander Grothendieck | title=Éléments de géométrie algébrique | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | edition=2nd | isbn=978-3-540-05113-8 | year=1971 | volume=1 | title-link=Éléments de géométrie algébrique }}, Chapter I.9</ref>

===Representable functor===
If <math>\mathcal E</math> is a [[quasi-coherent sheaf]] on a scheme <math>S</math> for a positive integer <math>k</math>, then to each <math>S</math>-scheme <math>T</math>, the Grassmannian functor associates the set of [[quotient module]]s of
:: <math>\mathcal{E}_T := \mathcal E \otimes_{O_S} O_T</math>
locally free of rank <math>k</math> on <math>T</math>. We denote this set by <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E}_T)</math>.

This [[functor]] is representable by a separated <math>S</math>-scheme <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E})</math>. The latter is [[Projective morphism#Affine and projective morphisms|projective]] if <math>\mathcal {E}</math> is finitely generated. When <math>S</math> is the spectrum of a field <math>K</math>, then the sheaf <math>\mathcal{E}</math> is given by a vector space <math>V</math> and the usual Grassmannian variety of the [[dual space]] of <math>V</math>can be recovered, namely: <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math>. By construction, the Grassmannian scheme is compatible with base changes: for any <math>S</math>-scheme <math>S'</math>, giving the canonical isomorphism
::<math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E} ) \times_S S' \simeq \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E}_{S'})</math>

In particular, for any point <math>s</math> of <math>S</math>, the canonical morphism <math>\{s\} = \text{Spec}K(s) \rightarrow S</math>
induces an isomorphism from the fiber <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal {E})_s</math> to the usual Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E} \otimes_{O_S} K(s))</math> over the [[residue field]] <math>K(s)</math>.

===Universal family===
Since the Grassmannian scheme represents a functor, it comes with a universal object, <math>\mathcal G</math>, which is an object of <math>\mathbf{Gr} \left (k, \mathcal{E}_{\mathbf {Gr}(k, \mathcal E)} \right),</math> and therefore a quotient module <math>\mathcal G</math> of <math>\mathcal E_{\mathbf {Gr}(k, \mathcal E)}</math>, locally free of rank <math>k</math> over <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E})</math>. The quotient [[homomorphism]] induces a [[closed immersion]] from the [[projective bundle]]:
::<math>\mathbf{P}(\mathcal G) \to \mathbf{P} \left (\mathcal E_{\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal E)} \right) = \mathbf P({\mathcal E}) \times_S \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal E). </math>

For any morphism of {{mvar|S}}-schemes:
::<math >T \to \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E}),</math>
this closed immersion induces a closed immersion
::<math> \mathbf{P}(\mathcal G_T) \to \mathbf{P} (\mathcal{E}) \times_S T.</math>

Conversely, any such closed immersion comes from a [[surjective]] homomorphism of <math>O_T</math>-modules from <math>\mathcal E_T</math> to a locally [[free module]] of rank <math>k</math>.<ref>[[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA]], II.3.6.3.</ref> Therefore, the elements of <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal E)(T)</math> are exactly the projective subbundles of rank <math>k</math> in <math >\mathbf{P} (\mathcal{E}) \times_S T.</math>

Under this identification, when <math>T=S</math> is the spectrum of a field <math> K</math> and <math>\mathcal E</math> is given by a vector space <math>V</math>, the set of rational points <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal{E})(K)</math> correspond to the projective linear subspaces of dimension <math>k-1</math> in <math>\mathbf{P}(V)</math>, and the image of <math>\mathbf{P}(\mathcal G)(K)</math> in
::<math display> \mathbf{P}(V) \times_K \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal E)</math>
is the set
::<math>\left\{ (x, v) \in \mathbf{P}(V)(K) \times \mathbf{Gr}(k, \mathcal E)(K) \mid  x\in v \right\}.</math>

== Plücker embedding ==
{{main|Plücker embedding}}

The [[Plücker embedding]]<ref name="GH">{{Citation | last1=Griffiths | first1=Phillip | author1-link=Phillip Griffiths | last2=Harris | first2=Joseph | author2-link=Joe Harris (mathematician) | title=Principles of algebraic geometry | page=211| publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] | location=New York | series=Wiley Classics Library | edition=2nd | isbn=0-471-05059-8 | mr=1288523 | year=1994 | zbl=0836.14001 }}</ref> is a natural embedding of the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)</math> into the projectivization of the <math>k</math>th [[exterior algebra#Exterior power|exterior power]] <math>\Lambda^k V</math> of <math>V</math>.
::<math display>\iota : \mathbf{Gr}(k, V) \to \mathbf{P} \left(\Lambda^k V \right ).</math>

Supposing that <math>w\subset V</math> is a <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace of the <math>n</math>-dimensional vector space <math>V</math>. To define <math>\iota(w)</math>, a basis <math> (w_1, \cdots, w_k)</math> for <math>w</math> can be chosen with <math>\iota(w)</math> as the projectivization of the wedge product of these basis elements:<math display="block">\iota(w) = [w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_k],</math>where <math> [ \, \cdot \, ]</math> denotes the projective equivalence class.

A different basis for <math>w</math> gives a different wedge product, but the two differ only by a non-zero scalar multiple (the [[determinant]] of the [[change of basis]] matrix). Since the right-hand side takes values in the projectivized space, <math>\iota</math> is well-defined. That it is an embedding, is shown by recovering <math>w</math> from <math>\iota(w)</math> as the [[linear span|span]] of the set of all vectors <math>v\in V</math> such that 
::<math> v \wedge \iota (w) = 0</math>.

=== Plücker coordinates and Plücker relations ===
The [[Plücker embedding]] of the Grassmannian satisfies simple quadratic relations called the [[Plücker embedding#Plucker relations|Plücker relations]]. These show that the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> embeds as a nonsingular projective algebraic subvariety of the projectivization <math>\mathbf{P}(\Lambda^k V)</math> of the <math>k</math>th exterior power of <math>V</math> and gives another method for constructing the Grassmannian. To state the Plücker relations, a basis <math>(e_1, \cdots, e_n)</math> for <math>V</math> is fixed, and <math>w\subset V</math> becomes a <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace of <math>V</math> with basis <math>(w_1, \cdots, w_k)</math>. <math>(w_{i1}, \cdots, w_{in})</math> becomes the components of <math>w_i</math> with respect to the chosen basis of <math>V</math>, and <math>(W^1, \dots, W^n)</math> the <math>k</math>-component column vectors forming the transpose of the corresponding homogeneous coordinate matrix:  
:: <math> W^T = [W^1\, \cdots W^n]= \begin{bmatrix} w_{11} &\cdots & w_{1n}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ w_{k1} & \cdots & w_{kn}
\end{bmatrix} ,</math>

For any ordered sequence <math>1\le i_1 < \cdots < i_k \le n</math> of <math>k</math> positive integers, <math>w_{i_1, \dots , i_k}</math> becomes the determinant of the <math>k \times k</math> matrix with columns <math>[W^{i_1}, \dots , W^{i_k}]</math>. The elements <math>\{w_{i_1, \dots , i_k} \, \vert \, 1 \leq i_1 < \cdots < i_k \leq n\}</math> are the [[Plücker coordinates]] of the element <math>w \in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> of the Grassmannian (with respect to the basis <math>(e_1, \cdots, e_n)</math> of <math>V</math>). These are the linear coordinates of the image <math>\iota(w)</math> of <math>w</math> under the Plücker map, relative to the basis of the exterior power <math> \Lambda^k V</math> space generated by the basis <math>(e_1, \cdots, e_n)</math> of <math>V</math>. Since a change of basis for <math>w</math> gives rise to multiplication of the Plücker coordinates by a nonzero constant (the determinant of the change of basis matrix), these are only defined up to projective equivalence, and hence determine a point in <math> \mathbf{P}(\Lambda^k V)</math>.

For any two ordered sequences <math>1 \leq i_1 < i_2 \cdots < i_{k-1} \leq n</math> and <math>1 \leq j_1 < j_2 \cdots < j_{k+1} \leq n</math> of <math>k-1</math> and <math>k+1</math> positive integers, respectively, the following homogeneous quadratic equations, known as the [[Plücker embedding#Plücker relations|Plücker relations]], or the [[Plücker embedding#Plücker relations|Plücker-Grassmann relations]], are valid and determine the image <math>\iota(\mathbf{Gr}_k(V))</math> of <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> under the Plücker map embedding:
:: <math>\sum_{l=1}^{k+1} (-1)^\ell w_{i_1, \dots , i_{k-1}, j_l} w_{j_1, \dots , \widehat{j_l}, \dots j_{k+1}} = 0,</math>

where <math>j_1, \ldots , \widehat{j_l}, \ldots j_{k+1}</math> denotes the sequence <math>j_1, \ldots, j_{k+1}</math> with the term <math>j_l</math> omitted. These are consistent, determining a nonsingular [[Projective variety|projective algebraic variety]], but they are not algebraically independent. They are equivalent to the statement that <math>\iota(w)</math> is the projectivization of a completely decomposable element of <math>\Lambda^k V</math>.

When <math>\dim(V) =4</math>, and <math> k=2</math> (the simplest Grassmannian that is not a projective space), the above reduces to a single equation. Denoting the homogeneous coordinates of the image <math>\iota(\mathbf{Gr}_2(V) \subset \mathbf{P}(\Lambda^2 V)</math> under the Plücker map as <math>(w_{12}, w_{13}, w_{14}, w_{23}, w_{24}, w_{34})</math>, this single Plücker relation is
::<math>w_{12}w_{34} - w_{13}w_{24} + w_{14}w_{23} = 0. </math>

In general, many more equations are needed to define the image <math>\iota(\mathbf{Gr}_k(V))</math> of the Grassmannian in <math> \mathbf{P}(\Lambda^k V)</math> under the Plücker embedding.

== Duality ==
Every <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace <math>W \subset V</math> determines an <math> (n-k)</math>-dimensional [[quotient vector space|quotient space]] <math>V/W</math> of <math>V</math>. This gives the natural [[short exact sequence]]:
::<math> 0 \rightarrow W \rightarrow V \rightarrow V/W \rightarrow 0.</math>

Taking the [[dual space|dual]] to each of these three spaces and the dual [[linear transformation]]s yields an inclusion of <math>(V/W)^*</math> in <math>V^*</math> with quotient <math>W^*</math>
::<math> 0 \rightarrow (V/W)^* \rightarrow V^* \rightarrow W^* \rightarrow 0.</math>

Using the natural isomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space with its double dual shows that taking the dual again recovers the original short exact sequence. Consequently, a one-to-one correspondence links <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>V</math> and <math>(n-k)</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>V^*</math>. In terms of the Grassmannian, this gives a canonical isomorphism
::<math> \mathbf{Gr}_k(V) \leftrightarrow \mathbf{Gr}_{n-k}(V^*)</math>

that associates to each subspace <math>W \subset V</math> its annihilator <math>W^0\subset V^*</math>. Choosing an isomorphism of <math>V</math> with <math>V^*</math> therefore determines a (non-canonical) isomorphism between <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k( V)</math> and <math>\mathbf{Gr}_{n-k}(V)</math>. An isomorphism of <math>V</math> with <math>V^*</math> is equivalent to the choice of an inner product, so with respect to the chosen inner product, this isomorphism of Grassmannians sends any <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace into its <math>(n-k)</math>-dimensional [[orthogonal complement]].

==Schubert cells==
{{see also|Schubert calculus}}
The detailed study of Grassmannians makes use of a decomposition into [[Affine space|affine subpaces]] called [[Schubert cell]]s, which were first applied in [[enumerative geometry]]. The Schubert cells for <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> are defined in terms of a specified [[flag (linear algebra)|complete flag]] of subspaces <math>V_1 \subset V_2 \subset \cdots \subset V_n=V</math> of dimension <math>\mathrm{dim}(V_i) = i</math>. For any [[integer partition]] 
: <math>\lambda =(\lambda_1, \cdots, \lambda_k)</math>
of weight
::<math>|\lambda|=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i</math>

consisting of weakly decreasing non-negative integers
:<math>\lambda_1 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_k \geq 0, </math> 
whose [[Young diagram]] fits within the rectangular one <math>(n-k)^k</math>, the Schubert cell <math>X_\lambda(k,n)\subset \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> consists of those elements <math>W \in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> whose [[intersection (set theory)|intersections]] with the subspaces <math>\{V_i\}</math> have the following dimensions
::<math> X_\lambda(k,n) = \{W \in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)\, | \, \dim(W \cap V_{n-k+j-\lambda_j}) = j\}. </math>

These are affine spaces, and their closures (within the [[Zariski topology]]) are [[Schubert varieties]].

As an example of the technique, determining the [[Euler characteristic]] <math>\chi_{k,n} </math> of the Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> of {{mvar|k}}-dimensional subspaces of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is illustrative. Fixing a <math>1</math>-dimensional subspace <math>\mathbf{R}\subset \mathbf{R}^n</math> and partitioning <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> into {{mvar|k}}-dimensional subspaces of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} that contain {{math|'''R'''}} and those that do not, reveals that the former is <math>\mathbf{Gr}_{k-1}(\mathbf{R}^{n-1})</math> and the latter is a rank <math>k</math> vector bundle over <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{R}^{n-1})</math>. This gives recursive formulae:
::<math> \chi_{k,n} = \chi_{k-1,n-1} + (-1)^k \chi_{k, n-1}, \qquad \chi_{0,n} = \chi_{n,n} = 1.</math>

Solving these [[recurrence relation|recursion relations]] gives the formula: <math>\chi_{k,n}=0</math> if <math>n</math> is [[parity (mathematics)|even]] and <math>k</math> is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] and
::<math>\chi_{k, n} = \begin{pmatrix}\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor \\ \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor
\end{pmatrix} </math>
otherwise.

===Cohomology ring===
Every point in the complex Grassmann manifold <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{C}^n)</math> defines a <math>k</math>-plane in <math>n</math>-space. Mapping each point in a k-plane to the point representing that plane in the Grassmannian yields the [[vector bundle]] <math>E</math>, which generalizes the [[tautological bundle]] of a [[projective space]]. Similarly the <math>(n-k)</math>-dimensional orthogonal complements of these planes yield an orthogonal vector bundle <math>F</math>. The integral [[cohomology]] of the Grassmannians is generated, as a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]], by the [[Chern class]]es of <math>E</math>. In particular, all of the integral cohomology is at even degree as in the case of a projective space.

These generators are subject to a set of relations, which defines the ring. The defining relations are easy to express for a larger set of generators, which consists of the Chern classes of <math>E</math> and <math>F</math>. Then the relations state that the [[direct sum of vector bundles|direct sum]] of the bundles <math>E</math> and <math>F</math> is trivial. [[Functor]]iality of the [[Chern class|total Chern classes]] shows that this relation is
::<math>c(E) c(F) = 1.</math>

The [[quantum cohomology]] ring was calculated by [[Edward Witten]].<ref name="Wi">{{cite arXiv |last1=Witten| first1= Edward | title =The Verlinde algebra and the cohomology of the Grassmannian | year=1993 | eprint= hep-th/9312104 }}</ref> The generators are identical to those of the classical cohomology ring, but with the top relation
::<math >c_k(E) c_{n-k}(F) = (-1)^{n-k}</math>
reflecting the existence in the corresponding [[quantum field theory]] of an [[instanton]] with <math>2n</math> fermionic [[Zero mode|zero-modes]], which violates the degree of the cohomology corresponding to a state by <math>2n</math> units.

==Associated measure==
When <math>V</math> is an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], a uniform measure on <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> can be defined. If <math>\theta_n</math> is the unit [[Haar measure]] on the [[orthogonal group]] <math> O(n)</math> and fix <math>w\in \mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math>, then for a set <math> A \subset\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> , 
::<math> \gamma_{k, n}(A) = \theta_n\{g \in \operatorname{O}(n) : gw \in A\}.</math>

This measure is invariant under the action of the group <math> O(n)</math>; that is,
::<math>\gamma_{k,n}(gA)= \gamma_{k,n}(A)</math>
for all <math>g \in O(n)</math>. Since <math>\theta_n(O(n))=1</math>, <math>\gamma_{k,n}(\mathbf{Gr}_k(V))= 1 </math>. Moreover, <math>\gamma_{k,n}</math> is a [[Radon measure]] with respect to the metric space topology and is uniform in the sense that every ball of the same radius (with respect to this metric) is of the same measure.

==Oriented Grassmannian==
This is the manifold consisting of all oriented <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math>. It is a double cover of <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)</math> and is denoted by <math>\widetilde{\mathbf{Gr}}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)</math>.

As a homogeneous space it can be expressed as:
:<math>\widetilde{\mathbf{Gr}}_k(\mathbf{R}^n)=\operatorname{SO}(n) / (\operatorname{SO}(k) \times \operatorname{SO}(n-k)).</math>

==Orthogonal isotropic Grassmannians==
Given a real or complex nondegenerate [[symmetric bilinear form]] <math>Q</math> on the <math>n</math>-dimensional space <math>V</math> (i.e., a scalar product), the totally isotropic Grassmannian <math>\mathbf{Gr}^0_k(V, Q)</math> is defined as the subvariety <math>\mathbf{Gr}^0_k(V, Q) \subset  \mathbf{Gr}_k(V) </math> consisting of all <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces <math>w\subset V</math> for which
:: <math> Q(u, v)=0, \, \forall \, u, v \in w, </math>

i.e., [[totally isotropic subspace]]s. [[Quadric (algebraic geometry)#Isotropic Grassmannians and the projective pure spinor variety|Maximal isotropic Grassmannians]] with respect to a real or complex scalar product are related to [[Élie Cartan|Cartan's]] theory of [[spinor]]s. Under the Cartan embedding, their connected components are equivariantly diffeomorphic to the projectivized minimal spinor orbit. Under the spin representation, the projective [[pure spinor]] variety which, similarly to the image of the [[Plucker embedding|Plücker map embedding]], is cut out as the intersection of a number of quadrics, becomes Cartan quadrics.<ref name="Ca">{{cite book | last1=Cartan | first1=Élie | title=The theory of spinors | orig-date=1938 | url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=0486640701 | publisher=[[Dover Publications]] | location=New York | isbn=978-0-486-64070-9 | mr=631850 | year=1981}}</ref><ref name="HS1">{{cite journal | last1=Harnad | first1=J. | last2=Shnider | first2=S. | title=Isotropic geometry and twistors in higher dimensions. I. The generalized Klein correspondence and spinor flags in even dimensions | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | publisher=American Institute of Physics | volume=33 | issue=9 | year=1992 |  doi=10.1063/1.529538 | pages=3197–3208| bibcode=1992JMP....33.3197H }}</ref><ref name="HS2">{{cite journal | last1=Harnad | first1=J. | last2=Shnider | first2=S. | title=Isotropic geometry and twistors in higher dimensions. II. Odd dimensions, reality conditions, and twistor superspaces   | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | publisher=American Institute of Physics | volume=36 | issue=9 | year=1995 |  doi=10.1063/1.531096 | pages=1945–1970 | bibcode=1995JMP....36.1945H | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Applications==
=== Pure mathematics ===
A key application of Grassmannians is as the "universal" embedding space for bundles with connections on compact manifolds.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Narasimhan | first1=M. S. |last2=Ramanan | first2= S. |year=1961 | title=Existence of Universal Connections | journal=American Journal of Mathematics | volume=83 |issue= 3  |pages= 563–572 | doi=10.2307/2372896 | jstor=2372896 | hdl=10338.dmlcz/700905 | s2cid=123324468 | hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Narasimhan | first1=M. S. |last2=Ramanan | first2= S. |year=1963 | title=Existence of Universal Connections II. | journal=American Journal of Mathematics | volume=85 |issue= 2  |pages= 223–231| doi=10.2307/2373211 | jstor=2373211 }}</ref>

Another important application is [[Schubert calculus]], which is the enumerative geometry involved in calculating the number of points, lines, planes, etc. in a projective space that intersect a given set of points, lines, etc., using the [[intersection theory]] of [[Schubert varieties]]. Subvarieties of Schubert cells can also be used to parametrize simultaneous eigenvectors of complete sets of commuting operators in quantum integrable spin systems, such as the [[Gaudin model]], using the [[Bethe ansatz]] method.<ref name="MTV">{{cite journal | last1=Mukhin | first1=E. | last2=Tarasov | first2=V. | last3=Varchenko | first3=A. | author3-link= Alexander Varchenko |title=Schubert Calculus and representations of the general linear group | journal=J. Amer. Math. Soc.  | publisher=American Mathematical Society | volume=22 | issue=4 | year=2009 | pages=909–940 |doi= 10.1090/S0894-0347-09-00640-7| doi-access=free | arxiv=0711.4079 | bibcode=2009JAMS...22..909M }}</ref>

=== Physics ===
A further application is to the solution of hierarchies of classical completely integrable systems of [[partial differential equations]], such as the [[Kadomtsev–Petviashvili equation]] and the associated [[Tau function (integrable systems)#Formal Baker–Akhiezer function and the KP hierarchy|KP hierarchy]]. These can be expressed in terms of [[Abelian group]] flows on an infinite-dimensional Grassmann manifold.<ref name="Sato">M. Sato, "Soliton equations as dynamical systems on infinite dimensional Grassmann manifolds", ''Kokyuroku, RIMS, Kyoto Univ.'', 30–46 (1981).</ref><ref name="DJKM1">{{cite journal | last1=Date | first1=Etsuro | last2=Jimbo | first2=Michio | last3=Kashiwara | first3=Masaki | last4=Miwa | first4=Tetsuji | title=Operator Approach to the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili Equation–Transformation Groups for Soliton Equations III– | journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan | publisher=Physical Society of Japan | volume=50 | issue=11 | year=1981 | issn=0031-9015 | doi=10.1143/jpsj.50.3806 | pages=3806–3812| bibcode=1981JPSJ...50.3806D }}</ref><ref name="DJKM2">{{cite journal | last1=Jimbo | first1=Michio | last2=Miwa | first2=Tetsuji | title=Solitons and infinite-dimensional Lie algebras | journal=Publications of the Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences | publisher=European Mathematical Society Publishing House | volume=19 | issue=3 | year=1983 | issn=0034-5318 | doi=10.2977/prims/1195182017 | pages=943–1001| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="HB1">{{cite book | last1=Harnad | first1= J. |  last2=Balogh | first2= F.  |author1-link=John Harnad |title=Tau functions and Their Applications, Chapts. 4 and 5 | year=2021 | series =Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics | publisher=Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, U.K. | isbn= 9781108610902 | doi=10.1017/9781108610902| s2cid= 222379146 }}</ref> The KP equations, expressed in Hirota bilinear form in terms of the [[Tau function (integrable systems)|KP Tau function]] are equivalent to the [[Plücker coordinates|Plücker relations]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sato |first1=Mikio |title=Soliton Equations as Dynamical Systems on Infinite Dimensional Grassmann Manifolds (Random Systems and Dynamical Systems) |url=http://hdl.handle.net/2433/102800 |journal=数理解析研究所講究録 |pages=30–46 |date=October 1981|volume=439 |hdl=2433/102800 }}</ref><ref name="HB1"/> A similar construction holds for solutions of the BKP integrable hierarchy, in terms of Abelian group flows on an infinite dimensional, maximal isotropic, Grassmann manifold.<ref name="DJKM1"/><ref name="DJKM2"/><ref name="HB2">{{cite book | last1=Harnad | first1= J. |  last2=Balogh | first2= F.  |author1-link=John Harnad |title=Tau functions and Their Applications, Chapt. 7 | year=2021 | series =Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics | publisher=Cambridge University Press | location = Cambridge, U.K. | isbn= 9781108610902 | doi=10.1017/9781108610902| s2cid= 222379146 }}</ref>

Finite dimensional positive Grassmann manifolds can be used to express [[soliton]] solutions of KP equations that are [[Singular point of an algebraic variety|nonsingular]] for real values of the KP flow parameters.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chakravarty |first1=S. |last2=Kodama |first2=Y. |title=Soliton Solutions of the KP Equation and Application to Shallow Water Waves |journal=Studies in Applied Mathematics |pages=83–151 |language=en |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9590.2009.00448.x |date=July 2009|volume=123 |issue=1 |s2cid=18390193 |arxiv=0902.4433 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kodama |first1=Yuji |last2=Williams |first2=Lauren |title=KP solitons and total positivity for the Grassmannian |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |pages=637–699 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00222-014-0506-3 |date=December 2014|volume=198 |issue=3 |bibcode=2014InMat.198..637K |s2cid=51759294 |arxiv=1106.0023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hartnett |first1=Kevin |title=A Mathematician's Unanticipated Journey Through the Physical World |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-mathematicians-adventure-through-the-physical-world-20201216/ |website=Quanta Magazine |date=16 December 2020 |access-date=17 December 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

The [[scattering amplitude]]s of [[subatomic particle]]s in maximally supersymmetric [[N = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory#Integrability|super Yang-Mills theory]] may be calculated in the planar limit via a positive Grassmannian construct called the [[amplituhedron]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Arkani-Hamed |first1=Nima |last2=Trnka |first2=Jaroslav |year=2013 |arxiv=1312.2007|title=The Amplituhedron |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2014 |issue=10 |page=30 |bibcode=2014JHEP...10..030A |doi=10.1007/JHEP10(2014)030 |s2cid=7717260 }}</ref>

In quantum chemistry and many-body quantum physics, the Grassmannian can be identified with the space of pure many-particle fermionic states which can be written as a single [[Slater determinant#Connection with Grassmann manifolds|Slater determinant]]. The geometric properties of the Grassmannian can be used to study theoretical properties of the [[Hartree-Fock]] method.<ref name="y938">{{cite journal | last1=Chiumiento | first1=Eduardo | last2=Melgaard | first2=Michael | title=Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds in quantum chemistry | journal=Journal of Geometry and Physics | volume=62 | issue=8 | date=2012 | doi=10.1016/j.geomphys.2012.04.005 | pages=1866–1881 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0393044012000927 | arxiv=1105.1661 }}</ref>

=== Computer science ===
Grassmann manifolds have found applications in [[computer vision]] tasks of video-based face recognition and shape recognition,<ref>Pavan Turaga, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Rama Chellappa: ''Statistical analysis on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds with applications in computer vision'', CVPR 23–28 June 2008, IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2008, {{ISBN|978-1-4244-2242-5}}, pp.&nbsp;1–8 ([https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4587733/;jsessionid=7D3470F21AC7B9C60781F9812A06BB54?arnumber=4587733 abstract], [http://www.public.asu.edu/~pturaga/papers/Manifolds.pdf full text])</ref> and are used in the data-visualization technique known as the [[Grand Tour (data visualisation)|grand tour]].

Grassmann flows are under consideration as a potential replacement for [[Attention (machine learning)|attention]] mechanisms in [[large language model]]s, based on research showing competitive performance with better computational efficiency and interpretability. Using low-dimensional subspaces on the Grassmann manifold, causal Grassmann layers allow:

* reducing token states to a lower dimension (e.g., from 256 to 32).
* encoding local token pairs as 2D subspaces using Plücker coordinates.
* fusing into hidden states through gated mixing, allowing information to "flow" via controlled deformations over multi-scale local windows.
* avoiding high-dimensional, pairwise tensor operations of standard self-attention, confining computations to a structured manifold for more traceable geometry.

In contrast to attention models, which process context at the scale of (O(n²)), Grassmann flows address scale linearly (O(n) for fixed subspace rank), enabling efficiency on long sequences without approximations like sparse attention.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Chong |first=Zhang |title=Attention Is Not What You Need |date=2025-12-22 |class=cs.LG |eprint=2512.19428}}</ref>

==See also==
*For an example of the use of Grassmannians in [[differential geometry]], see [[Gauss map#Generalizations|Gauss map]] 
*[[Flag manifold]]s are generalizations of Grassmannians whose elements, viewed geometrically, are nested sequences of subspaces of specified dimensions.
* [[Stiefel manifold]]s are bundles of orthonormal frames over Grassmannians. 
*Given a distinguished class of subspaces, one can define Grassmannians of these subspaces, such as [[Quadric (algebraic geometry)#Isotropic Grassmannians and the projective pure spinor variety|Isotropic Grassmannians]] or [[Lagrangian Grassmannian]]s.
*Grassmannians provide [[classifying space]]s in [[K-theory]], notably the [[classifying space for U(n)|classifying space for U(''n'')]]. In the [[homotopy theory |homotopy theory of schemes]], the Grassmannian plays a similar role for [[algebraic K-theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Morel | first1=Fabien | last2=Voevodsky | first2=Vladimir | author2-link=Vladimir Voevodsky | title=A<sup>1</sup>-homotopy theory of schemes | url=http://archive.numdam.org/article/PMIHES_1999__90__45_0.pdf | access-date=2008-09-05 | mr = 1813224 | doi = 10.1007/BF02698831 | year=1999 | journal=[[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]] | volume=90 | issn=1618-1913 | issue=90 | pages=45–143 | s2cid=14420180 }}, see section 4.3., pp.&nbsp;137–140</ref>
